claim_checks.locator_found: Vol. I, ch. 2 (Site descriptions: Kodumanal), p. 80; repeated p. 95
claim_checks.excerpt: In total, 1109 Tamiḻi (Tamil-Brahmi) inscribed potsherds (TU-PU 551+ASI 375+TNSDA 183= 1109) and 2622 (TU-PU 598 and TNSDA 2024= 2622; Data on ASI graffiti sherds are not available) graffiti bearing potsherds collected from the habitation cuttings
claim_checks.notes: p. 95: '1109 Tamiḻi inscribed potsherds came from Kodumanal, constituting 68.6% of the total inscribed potsherds coming from Tamil Nadu'.

claim_checks.excerpt: an inscribed potsherd reading visāki (re-read as visākanan) was collected from a transepted cist
claim_checks.notes: No interpretation is given at p. 80. p. 95 lists 'visā kanan' among 'personal names' found on Kodumanal sherds without saying whether it is this sherd; the knowledge base keeps 'not stated' for this object.

claim_checks.locator_found: Vol. II, preface pp. xi-xiii; ch. 7 'Tamiḻi inscribed potsherds: an introduction', p. 1075
claim_checks.excerpt: p. xi: 'Tamiḻi (Tamiḻ-Brāhmī/Damiḻi)'; p. xii: 'the Tamiḻi script, popularly called Tamiḷ-Brāhmī'; p. 1075: 'should be called as Tamiḻi. The term Damili is the Prakrit/corrupt form of Tamil.'
claim_checks.notes: The corpus uses 'Tamiḻi' throughout, as the claim says.

claim_checks.excerpt: p. 30: 'Excavations at Keeladi, Sivaganga District, Tamil Nadu'; p. 34: '(Tirupuvanam Taluk, Sivaganga District) was selected for systematic excavation'

p. 58: 'the site has yielded more than seventy Tamil-Brahmi inscribed potsherds and nearly six hundred graffiti sherds'; p. 63: 'About 70 Tamil-Brahmi inscribed pot sherds were collected from two field seasons.'
claim_checks.notes: p. 62: 'The post firing ligatured graffiti accounts for about six hundred sherds from both Locality I and II'.

claim_checks.excerpt: On the basis of stratigraphy and palaeographical grounds, these inscribed sherds may be dated to c. 2nd cent BCE - c. 1st cent CE.
claim_checks.notes: The S03 half of the claim (the ASI dating of its inscribed sherds) is found as stated. The TNSDA half (a 6th century BCE beginning) is attributed to R6 and was not checked here. The article also reports (p. 38) calibrated AMS dates 'ranging between 200 BC - 195 BC' for samples from 2.50 m and 1.95 m, and calls its period dates 'purely tentative'.

claim_checks.excerpt: p. 40: 'An inscribed pot sherd in Tamil-Brahmi in red ware lid was found at the depth of 2.36 meters reading ‘eravathan’.'; p. 63: names of individuals such as ... ‘eravathan’ (Figure16)
claim_checks.notes: The layer descriptions (pp. 39-40) belong to the Locality II trench YC1 (Figure 4, p. 39). The article also says (p. 63) that 'All the inscribed sherds came from Locality II coeval with the structural activities of Layer 2', which does not match the Layer 4/5 attributions of p. 40: an internal inconsistency of the article, for the verifier and expert to note.

claim_checks.excerpt: p. 62: 'Figure 17: Tamil – Brahmi Inscribed Black and Red Ware Dish ‘ce n ta n a va (ta) thi’'; p. 54: 'The label inscription below the shoulder of the dish bore the name of an individual probably its owner as ‘centan avathi’.'
claim_checks.differences: The knowledge base recorded the interpretation as 'not stated'. The article states it: the name of an individual, probably the owner (p. 54), and lists the reading as 'santhan avathi' (Figure 17) among names of individuals (p. 63). The reading itself is printed three ways: 'ce n ta n a va (ta) thi' (caption), 'centan avathi' (p. 54), 'santhan avathi' (p. 63). The knowledge-base entry was corrected on 2026-10-08 to record all three spellings and the printed interpretation; the correction is a transcription (transcribed_unverified), not a verification.
claim_checks.notes: Context as printed: an intact black and red ware dish found in situ inside the tank-like structure at about 1.00 m (p. 54).

claim_checks.excerpt: p. 40: 'At a depth of 2.16 meters another Tamil Brahmi inscribed sherd was found reading ‘sathan’.'; p. 63: 'The nature of these writing on the pottery was primarily aimed to register names of individuals probably its owner’s.'
